messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 36

The afternoon begins with a rupture. Six years ago, on a blistering July day, the pressurized canister gives way mid-application. Marcus, then sixty, watches the thick gray mist swallow the roof. He remembers the foreman’s shout, the sudden silence of the ventilation fans, the burning scratch in his throat. He drops to the shingles, clawing at a damp cloth mask with work-gloved hands. His lungs hitch. The crew drags him down the ladder, but the damage has already taken root. The physical healing takes months, but the air itself becomes hostile. Marcus tracks wind direction before stepping outside, eyes fixed on the horizon where the chemical plant sits. He stops sleeping through the night. When he finally drifts off, the weight of his own blankets feels like wet insulation pressing down on his chest. He wakes gasping, fingers instinctively reaching for a respirator that is no longer on his nightstand. His wife, Linh, learns to read the quiet alarms. She watches his jaw tighten when a distant truck backfires. She notices the sudden stillness that settles over him when the weather report mentions chemical transport on the interstate. He tells himself the worst is over, but he begins measuring out his morning routine with rigid precision, as if control could keep the past from seeping in. For a lifetime, his hands built shelter. He spent decades on sun-baked ridges, balancing tar kettles, pulling staples, and speaking a quiet language of grade lines and wind loads. In his family’s tradition, a man does not voice his fears, so he swallows the silence. The trauma does not erase that identity; it fractures it. At sixty-six, Marcus retires from the roofing crew, but the retirement should have brought relief. Instead, the quiet becomes a different kind of pressure. He walks the perimeter of his property twice a day, checking the downspouts and the fence line. He tells himself he is inspecting the drainage, but his eyes linger on the sky, waiting for the subtle shift in air that might carry something unnameable. The ground beneath his feet no longer feels solid. Every gust of wind carries a phantom weight, a reminder that safety was always temporary, bought with breath and exposure. He stops taking the long route to the market. He avoids the construction sites that still dot the suburban skyline, steering his truck wide around the cranes and tarps. The world has shrunk to a perimeter he can monitor, a space where he can trust what he sees instead of what he fears he will smell. When his grandchildren visit, he kneels in the yard to build elaborate block towers, but if a television commercial advertises industrial cleaners, his smile thins. He changes the channel before the audio cuts away. His hands, thickened and scarred from years of labor, now tremble slightly when he reaches for the garden hose, afraid the scent of damp rubber might pull him back to that afternoon. Linh knows not to ask about the old safety gear still stacked in the corner of his workshop. She has learned to sit quietly when his shoulders hunch at the sound of a neighbor’s pressure washer, or when he pauses mid-sentence, his gaze fixed on the garage door where a forgotten half-mask respirator still rests on a high shelf. He does not speak of the rupture. He does not need to. The tension in his forearms when the wind picks up, the careful economy of his movements through crowded grocery aisles, the quiet exhaustion that follows a simple trip to the hardware store—all of it maps a landscape he navigates alone. He moves through his days braced for the next shift in the air, conserving his energy for the moments when the past threatens to spill into the present.
